items.body: IUGA‘s debut album Meldrop is an intensely personal meditation on grief, nature and renewal, rooted in the forests of the Tuscan Apennines where the composer now lives. Inspired by the loss of his dog Toki and by the untamed landscape surrounding his home, the record traces an emotional journey in which wolves, deer, birds, snakes and humans inhabit the same fragile ecosystem. The title refers to the final drop left hanging from a runny nose after tears have run dry—a striking image that becomes a metaphor for grief persisting long after mourning appears to have subsided. There are no dramatic gestures here. The album is driven by atmosphere rather than narrative, favouring gradual shifts in mood over overt climaxes. “Unleash (Into la Rata)” immediately immerses the listener in unfamiliar territory, its fractured voices and restless modular textures creating a palpable sense of unease. “Toki” follows with a restrained lament whose melodic contours suggest farewell rather than despair. “Tail” picks up where the opening track leaves off, but with less disquiet. Having become acclimatised to the album’s sonic environment, the listener begins to find points of orientation. The tension returns in “Into Your Gaze”, where an electronically distorted voice seems to communicate from Hades. Yet expectations are constantly overturned. “Aspis” is unexpectedly calm and measured, acknowledging nature’s indifference without turning it into violence. Just when “Hurst” seems to open the possibility of tranquillity and reconciliation, the closing title track allows the drone to gather force before gradually dissipating, suggesting that grief never truly disappears but becomes part of one’s emotional landscape. Although Meldrop is created entirely with analogue and modular synthesis, it rarely feels technological. IUGA approaches his instruments instinctively, treating them almost as living organisms rather than machines. Recorded with minimal editing and almost no post-production, the album preserves the rawness of performance, allowing metallic resonances, unstable oscillations and breathing textures to evoke the physical presence of the forest itself. The result is a debut that resists sentimentality while remaining deeply affecting: an album in which grief is neither conquered nor romanticised, but gradually absorbed into the wider rhythms of the natural world. To shed further light on Meldrop, IUGA kindly answered a few questions by email. Meldrop is described as an album about the place you call home, your dogs, the forest and the lives that inhabit it. The record often feels like an ecosystem in which different forms of life coexist. How did the landscape around you shape the music, and were there specific encounters, sounds or memories that found their way into an album which, as the liner notes indicate is, at least partially, shaped by personal grief? Meldrop is deeply connected to the place where I’ve been living for about four years now, a magical, wild spot in the mountains outside Florence. I can say with certainty that without this place, this album wouldn’t exist. The opening track, “Unleash (Into la Rata),” marks my entrance into the house in the woods. I finally felt free, unleashed, but also overwhelmed by the wilderness and the life thriving within it. I tried to convey in music the sensation of wolves pushing up to the thresholds of my home and their howling at dusk, echoing across the entire valley. The spectacular concert of nocturnal birds, whose spectral songs accompanied me to sleep, the sheer wonder of rediscovering hundreds, thousands of fireflies after so many years, having believed they were gone forever. The meaning of Meldrop is “a drop at the tip of the nose / a runny nose”, and it’s tied to the loss of my dog, which happened the year after I moved here. The entire album revolves around this, and the track “Toki” is dedicated to her, or rather, to us. It’s my farewell, her funeral, the moments leading up to her burial, when I carried her in my arms from my house to the spot I had chosen just a few meters away. In that moment, those few meters felt like hundreds of kilometers, and when even the tears had run dry, only that drop at my nose, that meldrop, was left. It stayed with me for hours, days, even months. That’s why I speak of a fragile emotional reconstruction, so much of my energy in the following months was spent finding myself again, forgiving myself, and rebuilding a new beginning. Toki died from an asp bite; in my mind, the track “Aspis” tells the story of that day when their paths crossed, and consequently, mine did too. The sound builds up in a crescendo, its intensity rising to a climax that marks the final, fatal strike by the viper. It took a long time to understand that nature is also this, that awe and wonder don’t just manifest in its beauty, but also in its cruelty, and that there is no right or wrong in nature. Everything is in its place, every life follows its course. The album explores birth, life, death and what you describe as a realm where “even death becomes solely a matter of sound and scent.” That is a striking image. How did you approach translating such deeply physical and sensory experiences into a language of modular synthesis and ambient composition, especially when working without conventional narrative or lyrics? Also, what do the vocals concealed in the track “Into your gaze” refer to? Are they intedend as a warning? Modular synthesis was the only necessary path for composing these tracks, it allows me to know myself deeply and establish a conversation with my inner self. I always say that I don’t play my instruments, but rather I play with them, manipulating and letting myself be manipulated by the living sound, so as to respect its intrinsic, primal electricity. Since this is a deeply personal album, I needed to feel completely honest, first and foremost with myself, but also with the listener. I tried to convey my lived experience, my emotions, and the surrounding environment through these “machines,” often letting myself sink into long nighttime sessions lasting hours and hours, solely in search of sonorities that would come into contact with the most hidden and fragile part of me, the part that ultimately gave birth to the album. “Into Your Gaze” is a very difficult track for me to analyze, somewhat like the entire album. If you try to analyze everything you won’t come out a winner, but if you let yourself be carried away, you do. I’ll try to help with a cinematic example from one of my favorite directors, Lars von Trier. In a scene from the film Antichrist, the protagonist, during one of his frequent walks in the woods, spots among the vegetation a wounded and bloodied fox. The animal lies hidden, biting and tearing at its own flesh, self-devouring. Turning its gaze toward the protagonist, it roars in an infernal voice: “Chaos reigns.” With “Into Your Gaze,” I wanted to convey that exact same sensation you get when watching that scene. I wanted to show the dark, infinitely powerful side of nature that doesn’t obey human logic, and that is very often governed by a blind destructiveness to which the human being can only submit. The title, on the other hand, in contrast to these dark forces, comes from my encounters in the woods with wild animals, especially deer, foxes and, more rarely, nocturnal birds of prey. There is a moment when our eyes lock, and I am in your gaze, and you are in mine. In that precious moment, I vanish, I am matter, I am nature. It’s a gesture of light that touches my core and restores my balance. The same goes, though on a more frequent basis, with my dogs. Being in their gaze makes me feel at home every single time. Toki Although Meldrop is built entirely from analogue and modular synthesizers, it rarely feels technological. Instead, it conveys something organic, almost animalistic, as if the machines themselves were breathing or responding to the environment. What attracts you to modular synthesis as a tool for expressing themes of nature, grief and memory, and how much of the album emerged through improvisation versus careful construction? I’m really glad that this feeling comes through. This wild imagery stems directly from the nature I inhabit, and managing to convey something organic and animalistic, as you say, was the goal of this album from the very start. I believe much of this result is due to my approach with modular synthesis: I have a deep aversion to academic studying and technicalities, I hate reading manuals, and I hate practicing by studying every single module and its specifications. I let myself be guided by the sound, I explore like a child on an adventure. I delve into the search for sounds in an animalistic way, yes, guided by instinct and primal need. It’s just like when I abandon myself in the woods with my dogs: we are part of the environment, we take our time to scout around, respecting the place we are in and its inhabitants. In the exact same way, I respect the sound and my creative process, without forcing anything, without planning a single thing. I step into my sonic forest and let myself be cradled. No, there was no meticulous construction at all, quite the opposite, in fact. I recorded everything on an old, heroic computer from 2006 that can barely run the recording software, let alone heavy modern plug-ins. This self-imposed limitation helped me get straight to the heart of my sounds, which are intentionally rudimentary, with an almost metallic and primitive feel. There was very little, almost zero, multitrack recording, no sampled sounds (except for the vocal recording on “Into Your Gaze”), and minimal post-production. Even regarding the opening track “Unleash (Into la Rata),” the quasi-animal shouts echoing through it are entirely produced by modular synths, specifically by the Tabor oscillator from the Italian brand Jolin Lab. It was essential for me to create every single sound through careful research and experimentation. The cover artwork by Bernardo Lupo Migone is immediately arresting: a solitary figure suspended in free fall, caught somewhere between descent and flight. It seems to resonate strongly with the album’s themes of loss, transformation and surrender to forces beyond one’s control. How did that image become associated with Meldrop, and what does the falling figure represent to you in relation to the music? When I saw that image for the first time I immediately said, “there it is, I found it”. It’s an incredibly strong, high-impact image. The caption read, “A body moves through space and time”, and that’s exactly it. This suspended figure is still, yet it moves. I was fascinated by the fact that it could be interpreted in different ways. For instance, some might see it as a fall, while others see it as a leap into the void, intentional, brave, and liberating. In any case, the time had come for me to fall; the moment had arrived to free myself from certain fears I had been dragging around for too long, to heal from the grief of losing my beloved dog, and to deeply embrace my pain. To embrace this “mal di vivere”, this existential malaise, that too often has been a heavy burden, deciding for once to transform it into something beautiful through my music. Bernardo Lupo Migone is a talented photographer and a delightful person who was immediately supportive and enthusiastic about being part of the project. Without his imagery, the album wouldn’t have carried the same meaning; he made this debut of mine even more special. Finally, I would like to thank Raffaele Pezzella, founder and curator of the label Unexplained Sounds Group, who believed in this project from the very first listen. He showed courage and intellectual integrity, evaluating solely the quality of my work rather than who I was, how many followers I had, how many albums I had produced, or how many “cool” places I had played. He believed in my music, and given the times we live in, that is something we can’t take for granted. Emerging artists need exactly this: someone who believes in their project regardless of who you are or the numbers you pull. There is a need for truth, to rediscover the essence of sound. There is a need to give voice and support to those who deserve a release through their music and not through the construction of a persona. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Empire of Sand provides impeccably built darkened droning soundscapes with an emotional and nihilistic apex. The whole sonic architecture is centered on assaultive, multi-layered harsh electric guitar patterns; micro-noisy, grainy ambient electronics; and a grandiose, spellbinding dystopian cinematic component. Dedicated to the defense of extreme music Ksenza Records is an undisputed key indie label dedicated to the defense of extreme music, from merciless (post-)metal subgenres to deep ambient music, electro-cinematic spells, and abstract noise. I’m familiar with part of their catalogue, including releases by Nytt Land, who have also published major works on Cold Spring (U.K.), as well as Sutekh Hexen and Thisquietarmy. This collaborative effort is the result of a groundbreaking artistic meeting between Nimh (the project of pioneering Italian post-industrial and ethno-ritual drone musician Giuseppe Verticchio) and Sleepwalker (the project of the mastering engineer behind Ksenza). Empire of Sand provides impeccably built darkened droning soundscapes with an emotional and nihilistic apex. The whole sonic architecture is centered on assaultive, multi-layered harsh electric guitar patterns; micro-noisy, grainy ambient electronics; and a grandiose, spellbinding dystopian cinematic component. The brooding and elegantly evocative moving pieces lead the listener into a dense metaphysical post-human world surrounded by decaying fortresses, aural figures from the past, forlorn mythological creatures, ghoulish presences, and tearful angels. Some moments of lightness and serenity occasionally emerge from the desolate, isolationist sensorial bath, as in the elegiac gothadelic anthem “Empire of Sand” and the ascending “The Endless Journey.” The perfect bleak soundtrack for an immersion into ominous sci-fi novels depicting subterranean, cold, anguished, demonic, fearful, and paroxysmal worlds at the border between real and imaginary time, notably found in the classic books of M. P. Shiel, C. Ashton Smith, N. Henneberg, and R. W. Chambers. An awe-inspiring album that is a highly recommended addition for those who enjoy mystical and dark musical odysseys where organic ambient meets drone metal and entrancing noise. Fans of Monocube, Shrine, Nadja, Locrian, Khanate, and similar artists won’t be disappointed. Empire of Sand is available on Ksenza. [Bandcamp] Empire of Sand by Nimh/SleepwalkerThe post Nimh/Sleepwalker :: Empire of Sand (Ksenza) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Each Monolake release is, of course, sui generis with a context and sound never to recur, but Interstate is unique in its way—document of a vital musical and cultural moment capturing paradigm shifts in (pre-)millennial music production; its deep textured electronics and ever-morphing cyber-rhythms a snapshot of two phonauts boundary-surfing with then cutting edge tech, causing ripples that became waves that would break over the ’00s and beyond. Interstate teems with insectoid detail and dizzying depth of field Interstate by Monolake   The ’90s: an arena for innovative endeavor, in electronic music more than most domains, a simultaneously post- and pre- context eliciting hark-back feed-forward works from e.g. Aphex Twin, Autechre and Boards of Canada that felt, differently, futurist. Likewise Zeitgeist-wise was Interstate, dub techno/ambient electronica duo Monolake’s second album—the last with Gerhard Behles, who left here (1999) to focus on developing the ground-breaking Ableton Live, leaving Robert Henke solo. It started at Technische Universität Berlin—two programming students, early adopters in a burgeoning digital scene, writing music in Max. It would influence the local scene in Berlin and beyond, preparing the ground for Ableton Live—1999 also saw Ableton founded by Henke and Behles with software engineer Bernd Roggendorf. The rest is Geschichte… In this light then may be seen the choice of Interstate as first vinyl in Field Records’ Monolake reissue program. Truly seminal, essential for dub techno and ambient electronica heads alike, along with the reissues of Hong Kong (2008) (see igloo-‘view), compiling the early Chain Reaction EPs, and Gravity (2025) (see igloo-’view); among the most idiosyncratic works where dub techno, microsound and hyperreal electronica intersect, the duo cemented a vision of a quasi-organic post-techno crossing club-home-’phones via a custom sound design and syncopated beats mix. Max/MSP enabled envelope-pushing into vibrant forms where rhythm and sound move in mysterious ways. “Abundance” sets tone, gaseous atmo solidifying into click-y rhythmicity, whirrs and judders cycling echoically into the aether in a fuzz-wash haze. “Gecko”’s full-on techery creates almost total mechanicity (mechanicCity?), electric chirp meshing with birdsong bleeps. “Tangent I” and “Tangent II” hitch roiling low-end to layered synth, “I” with liquid textures like digital drizzle and chattering percussive hiss, “II” with heftier metallic parts, its head-nod slashed with springy stabs. “Perpetuum”’s electro pong workout cedes to “Amazon”’s tract of neo-virtual reality, then “Ginza” and “Terminal” abstract d’n’b geometry into a sleek dub-inflected design. Throughout Interstate teems with insectoid detail and dizzying depth of field, the two like Circe in circuitry conjuring from code immersive spaces as deft in kinesis as they are questing in timbre. Each Monolake release is, of course, sui generis with a context and sound never to recur, but Interstate is unique in its way—document of a vital musical and cultural moment capturing paradigm shifts in (pre-)millennial music production; its deep textured electronics and ever-morphing cyber-rhythms a snapshot of two phonauts boundary-surfing with then cutting edge tech, causing ripples that became waves that would break over the ’00s and beyond. Interstate is available on Field Records. [Bandcamp] Interstate by Monolake  The post Monolake :: Interstate (Remastered) (Field) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: This music tells of the passage of time, with sparse humorous and facetious tones punctuating the moodier ensemble. Each track is elaborated and designed as a subtle, sentient vignette in the mind of a daydreaming smoker and ordinary thinker who opens his soul and invites the listener to witness his hope, fear, despair, and intricate yet playful reflections. A slow journey through existential wandering 20 Cigarettes by Jesper Møller Nielsen   French indie net label with a substantial production, navigating from lo-fi electronics and leftfield minimalism to noisy soundscapes and atmospheric alt-pop, Lotophagus Records offers here a new album by guitarist and sound explorer Jesper Moller Nielsen. The compositions are based on the spoken words and personal diary of multidirectional intermedia artist Jordane Prestrot, known for his essentially narrative-focused experimental works, often using poetry and irony as their main ingredients. The album evolves as a slow journey through existential wandering, anecdotal and reflective situations. Each smoked cigarette represents a distinct personal life moment, suggesting a state of mind and various encounters with oneself. The minimal, deliberately rough-hewn guitar patterns are articulated around thoughts translated through spoken words, while various sonic explorations, effects, and processed field recordings enhance the album’s narrative purpose. This music tells of the passage of time, with sparse humorous and facetious tones punctuating the moodier ensemble. Each track is elaborated and designed as a subtle, sentient vignette in the mind of a daydreaming smoker and ordinary thinker who opens his soul and invites the listener to witness his hope, fear, despair, and intricate yet playful reflections. There is something in this album that evokes the literary wanderings and explorations of consciousness found in Italo Svevo. In itself, the music and its fragmented, bluesy melodies in slow motion suggest feelings akin to those found in road movies, notably the films of Jim Jarmusch. 20 Cigarettes is recommended for fans of desolate guitar microsounds, field recordings, and evocative, semi-improvised ambiences in the spirit of Loren Connors & David Grubbs, Western Grey, Luca Nasciuti, and Sqürl. 20 Cigarettes is available on Lotophagus. [Bandcamp] 20 Cigarettes by Jesper Møller NielsenThe post Jesper Møller Nielsen :: 20 Cigarettes (Lotophagus) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Olùsìn [Worshippers] moves with the gravity of a procession seen from a great distance: slow synth masses, vocal apparitions, soft percussive grammar, low harmonic pressure, field material absorbed into the body of the music. TEXT Olùsìn [Worshippers] by Ibukun sunday   Lagos born, North London based violist, sound artist and electronic composer Ibukun Sunday has slowly shaped one of the most singular languages in contemporary Afro ambient music. His path begins in classical discipline, with viola study from childhood and ensemble experience across chamber and orchestral settings, then opens into field recording, live electronics, noise texture, synthesizer sound and a personal idea of music as spiritual perception. Earlier releases for Phantom Limb’s Spirituals imprint, including The Last Wave and Mantra, placed him in dialogue with philosophy, apocalypse, Vedic thought and Nigerian memory; Harmony / Balance, issued in 2024, carried that research into a wider frame, where drone, melody and existential inquiry moved as a single organism. Olùsìn [Worshippers] now gives this practice its most concentrated form. The album is presented as a devotional ambient work rooted in West African rhythmic tradition, and the definition is useful only as an entrance. Sunday is dealing with faith as vibration, with praise as a form of breath made audible. The record moves with the gravity of a procession seen from a great distance: slow synth masses, vocal apparitions, soft percussive grammar, low harmonic pressure, field material absorbed into the body of the music. Everything advances through recurrence. Motifs return as if memory had learned to sing in circles. Rhythm rarely asks for attention directly; it glows under the surface, ticks inside consonants, gathers in small pulses, then expands into a shared heartbeat. “Rhythm rarely asks for attention directly; it glows under the surface, ticks inside consonants, gathers in small pulses, then expands into a shared heartbeat.” ~Mirco Salvadori What makes Olùsìn [Worshippers] so persuasive is the way Sunday refuses decorative spirituality. The music carries devotion through craft. The choral tones are gauzy and spectral, yet their placement feels almost architectural. The bass frequencies hold a stern calm, the upper harmonics shimmer with a pale organ light, and the voices seem less like singers than traces of people gathered in the same act of listening. At moments the album approaches the suspended radiance of church music, at others it returns to earth through grain, breath, thud and sampled speech. The sacred quality comes through pressure and patience, through the decision to let each sound reveal its weight. A record of rare poise: luminous, grounded, inwardly ecstatic :: Across the eight pieces, Sunday treats the studio as a vessel for collective energy. The titles suggest elemental conditions: whisper, echo, amen, breeze, ages, devotion, hill, edge. They function as points in a wider rite of perception, each one carrying a small emotional temperature. The opening half favors deep resonance and vocal haze, with melodies rising like thin beams through the darkened density of the drones. The central section grows warmer, richer, almost tactile, allowing the listener to sense the body behind the electronics. Toward the final stretch, plucked synthetic figures and trembling harmonic patterns introduce a sharper contour, as if prayer had become a lattice of light. “Amen,” already chosen as the first public signal from the record, offers the clearest key to Sunday’s method. A vocal fragment, full of sibilant motion and West African cadence, becomes rhythm before it becomes meaning. Around it, the synths swell with organ like solemnity, and the piece turns into a compact ceremony of ascent. Edge, near the end, works through Karplus Strong pizzicato logic, its plucked particles layering into a bright, nervous mesh. These moments reveal how Sunday thinks: he begins from pulse, timbre, oral memory and instrumental knowledge, then lets technology behave like a devotional instrument. The machine serves breath, fingers, choir, dust, air. “For an American listener trained by the genealogies of minimalism, gospel resonance, fourth world drift, post Eno ambient and contemporary sound art, Sunday’s record opens a different line of descent.” ~Mirco Salvadori There is also a quiet severity in this album. Its beauty arrives through restraint. Sunday’s classical background is audible in his sense of proportion, in the way he allows harmonic fields to bloom, fade, gather again, and in the discipline with which he keeps the palette reduced. Many ambient records seek immersion through endless expansion; Olùsìn [Worshippers] achieves depth through measure. It feels carved from a few essential elements, each one placed where silence can give it force. The percussion is subtle, the voices are veiled, the field recordings are folded into the fabric, and the melodic cells move with the humility of repeated prayer. For an American listener trained by the genealogies of minimalism, gospel resonance, fourth world drift, post Eno ambient and contemporary sound art, Sunday’s record opens a different line of descent. Its center is West African, diasporic, devotional, intimate, communal. It carries the discipline of the violist, the patience of the field recordist, the concentration of the producer and the listening ethics of an artist who has spoken of sound as a soul language. Olùsìn [Worshippers] asks for attention as participation. It turns worship into acoustic matter, praise into frequency, solitude into chorus. In doing so, Ibukun Sunday has made a record of rare poise: luminous, grounded, inwardly ecstatic, and quietly radical in its faith that sound can still carry human presence beyond explanation. Olùsìn [Worshippers] is available on Phantom Limb. [Bandcamp] Olùsìn [Worshippers] by Ibukun sunday   The post Ibukun Sunday :: Olùsìn [Worshippers] (Phantom Limb) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: In 2024, Elaha Soroor and members of Kefaya performed at a celebration of Hazara culture in Vienna, where posters advertising the event were torn from walls across the city, in what read as an attempt to silence it. The Hazara are a mostly Shia minority who have endured more than a century of persecution in Afghanistan, much of the community scattered into exile, which is why celebrating that culture abroad can still draw hostility. “A Bright Gaze – Negahe Roshan” came out of what followed: the solidarity and unexpected friendships that gathered around the musicians. It is the one bright stretch on Our Freedoms Must Be Won – Azadi Kho Bigri, an album otherwise built on exile and displacement, out this July on the band’s own label, Radio International. The track is built on a 7/8 Afghan folk rhythm, then set inside a synth-rock frame. The guitar carries folk and blues inflections over a warm bank of analogue synthesiser, while synth lines answer Soroor’s voice in call-and-response. The band put the arrangement together through improvisation, which gives it a quick, unforced momentum. Soroor grew up between Iran and Afghanistan and rose to national attention as a finalist on the television contest Afghan Star, the first female Hazara singer to perform on Afghan television. After she used her platform to condemn the stoning law, death threats forced her out of the country, and she rebuilt her music in London. Kefaya, the London trio of guitarist Giuliano Modarelli, keys player Al MacSween and drummer Joost Hendrickx, take their name from the Arabic word for enough, a cry that ran through the Arab Spring. Modarelli and MacSween started the group in 2012 and built their 2016 debut, Radio International, from sessions tracked across India, Palestine, Italy and Spain, wiring folk traditions to electronics and threading political voices through the mix. They first worked with Soroor on 2019’s Songs of Our Mothers, reworking Afghan women’s songs into something harder and more electronic. Stream “A Bright Gaze” HERE, and get a copy of Our Freedoms Must Be Won on vinyl and digital through THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Kefaya & Elaha Soroor – A Bright Gaze appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by yarstruly — Clicked 4, but really a bit better at 4.25.Let's call this one, back to "Bass-ics" as this album features three of the world's top bassists in a collaboration called "Dystopia". Alberto Rigoni (Jeff Scott Soto, Jordan Rudess, Marco Minnemann, Gavin Harrison), Michael Manring (Spastic Ink, Alex Skolnik/Skol Patrol, Attention Deficit, Steve Morse, Alex De Grassi, Will Ackerman and others) and Stuart (Stu) Hamm (Steve Vai, Joe Satriani, Frank Gambale) are the bassists and they are augmented by drummers Tim "Herb" Alexander (Primus) and David Menoudakis (Motion Device). Rigoni is the album's producer.The album comes courtesy of the all-around awesome guy Nick Katona (the man has style!) and his label Melodic Revolution Records (MMR). It was released on February 27, 2026. I look forward to reviewing more music released by this label. As always, this is a cold listen, I receive no additional compensation, and I call it like I hear it. The only frame of reference I have going into this is "Fish Out of Water" by the late, great Chris Squire, but this album is a fully instrumental affair, so it should be interesting. Without further ado, let's get down deep into it.Track 1 - Genesis (4:26)A moderately slow chordal pattern starts off the track, and a cool drum groove comes in with a polyrhythmic pattern. At around 1 minute in, they lock into a groove. They are using some effects that make some of the bass notes sound almost brass-like; very cool. The drums play some amazing fills. The groove changes at around 3:25. I don't know which bassist is playing what, but there was a cool lead break near the ending. Great tune!Track 2 - The Algorithm (3:16)This begins with droning sounds, onto which a fretless bass plays an opening tune. So far there are no drums on this and it is very atmospheric. I wonder if one or more of them is using a synth pickup module to create some of these sounds. Nice soundscape track.Track 3 - Entropia (3:55)This one has a jazzy groove to it, with shifting meters. It's very proggy! Lots of great rhythms here. There is a melodic hook. Cool bass and drum synchronicity at around 3:20 on a morse code rhythm. I like it!Track 4 - Limbo (3:59)This fades in with some foreboding sounds. No drums on this one. There is a sense of motion, however, caused by the rhythms. One of the basses takes on a piano-like tone. There are some unique effects in the later part of the track. Pretty interesting.Track 5 - Solar (3:27)I like the descending, chord-melody thing that they start with here. The drums are back in a big way here. I like the changing melodies and grooves throughout this track. These guys are definitely among the best in the world and are showing it on this track. Great drum solo after 3 minutes. One of my favorites from the album, I'd say!Track 6 - Ethereal Horizon (2:34)Bass harmonics are featured as this one begins. The synth-like tones are back; maybe a whammy pedal? They are certainly re-defining what the bass can do here. Track 7 - Dystopia (8:46)The final/title track is the longest, so let's call it a closing epic. A rhythm pattern with drums is established quickly. At around 1:30 one of the guys takes on a lead guitar type tone, which is later harmonized with another player; they use a distortion effect. Following that, there is a really cool canon-like section with the three playing overlapping tunes. Great drum grooves on this as well. They really take us through several grooves and moods. I love the groove that kicks in at around the 5-minute mark. I like the slow harmonies as they approach the 7-minute mark; gradually all 3 of them take part in the chords, and there are overdubs as well as it keeps building. It is a rich, brassy tone they are creating. The bass can create many timbres and they show it here. The only thing missing for me is a final punctuation for the ending, as it just kind of stopped. Otherwise, this is clearly the flag-ship track of the album.OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:This is a fairly short album at around 31 minutes, perhaps we should call it an EP. Regardless, this is an entertaining way to spend half an hour and see what three master-bassists (sorry, I'll go sit in the corner now?) can do. It was an interesting experiment and yielded some cool results. I have no Idea whether they are planning to follow-up with more releases, but it's worth checking out. I'll give this a respectable 4.25 out of 5, or 85%. Thanks again to Nick Katona and MRR for providing me with this music for review. I expect there be more in the not-too-distant future.

items.body: Review by XixoTheRock — Locande delle fate is a band which I had not heard of until an acquaintance of mine recommended themto me after chatting about prog and jazz for a while, evidently as I do, I postponed listening toany of their records until I finished some pending ones, now I have listened to this record, "HomoHomini Lupus" twice, and I'm eager to say the many things I think about this particular record,which, are not very positive if I'm to be very honest.I'd like to address that, I do not speak Italian, and while Spanish and Italian do share a ton ofgrammar, words and common origin from latin, I did not fully understand the lyrics because of thislanguage barrier, judging by the overview I did indeed understand, this is a concept album, which isapparent and obvious mainly by the track titles, despite this, I will not analyze the lyrical aspectof the record any further since I'm not in a position to do so.This record is quite different from your average RPI record in the sense that, it's notgrandiloquent, baroque, theatrical and Mediterranean sounding, I'd like to say that something thatmakes a record great is sticking to it's cultural roots and sound while innovating and expandingit's foundations...Homo Homini Lupus DOES NOT do that, it splits from the Italian roots that madeRPI great in the first place, and tries to mimic Anglo-Saxon rock and pop. The quality of thecompositions is very poor, the tracks are mostly bland and dull, nothing really fits completely, itsits in an uncanny valley : trying to mimic someone else while trying to pretend you have notabandoned your identity. The instruments are simple, just hour typical line up of some keys,guitars, bass guitars and drums, sometimes less is more, but this is not the case, they feeldisconnected both musically and emotionally...almost as a watered down Alan Parsons project, which Iwill asume was a big inspiration for Locanda delle fate's creative process.Despite the musicians and singer being very talented, they still feel plain, they sound as if theywere not motivated, the singer's high pitched vocals are also unbearable most of the time, they trybeing dramatic..maybe they tried TOO hard, and too much of anything is never any good.The production is also dull, not balanced, poorly equalized, inconsistent between tracks (whichworsens the fact that all songs, are almost the same in composition, and this productioninconsistency does not help at all), and the guitar tones are simply just too exaggerated.For the quality this record has, it could have been 10 or 15 minutes shorter and no one wouldcomplain really, it's a record that disappoints, specially since it is part of one of the best progsub genres...really, I wouldn't listen to it again, and I urge you that, if you want to listen toany other record by Locanda delle fate, follow the advice of other reviewers and avoid this record,go straight into their debut album.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Echoes And Signals: a blend of techno-prog-math and experimental post-new-wave?or at least, that's how I like to describe them."Simulacra" begins with a brooding atmosphere?wailing guitars and a melancholic sound blending post-rock, math-rock, and crossover styles with a touch of Wilson-esque psychedelia. It's a musical treat to whet the appetite. "Temporal Waves" shifts into dark electro, a monolithic cinematic soundscape weaving through danceable electronics to create a contemplative mood. The guitar solo echoes Porcupine Tree, with notes bursting forth alongside a great riff and an expansive shredding section reminiscent of Randy McStine, all leading into an outro driven by an immersive looper effect. "Cloud Gallery" deepens the atmospheric, spacey sound; the vocals?reminiscent of Radiohead or Eno?float over a backdrop of reverberating synths. A bewitching, groovy guitar dialogue takes hold, leading to an explosive finale driven by a heavy riff and solemn, almost liturgical vocals."Evermore" features acoustic guitar and atmospheric spoken-word vocals, with radiant keyboards; there's a hint of Barclay James Harvest in the mellow, sentimental vibe, while the western-style tones lend a space-psych lament quality. "Singularity" is built on a moody electronic foundation, with accessible synths complementing the soft, melodic guitar. A gradual build-up launches a smooth, captivating crescendo, with Fedor's vocals vibrating with a nonchalant, reverent intensity. At the halfway mark, the musical momentum shifts?a "Berlin School" atmosphere triggers an energetic detour, featuring a long, driving passage where Leo's presence is frantically felt. It concludes with a robotic, vocoded finale set against chilling synths reminiscent of Tangerine Dream?truly surprising.Echoes And Signals represents a philosophical-musical translation?a concept of opposites for an album that exists in the space between, capturing fragments of a shifting reality. A sound that leans towards dark wave, electro, and cinematic post-rock?echoes and signals indeed!

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — With Phil Miller, Pip Pyle, Amanda Parsons, Jimmy Hastings, and the very architect of the Canterbury scene, Dave Stewart, all members of Hatfield and the North, National Health was formed, joined by bassist Neil Murray, who came from Colosseum II and would also work with Bill Bruford during the rehearsals for Feels Good to Me.Right from the start with "Tenemos Roads," there is a distinct energy, stemming from a rhythm section (drums and bass) that leans toward aggressive jazz-rock fusi�n, to which Jimmy Hastings' bass clarinet adds a supernatural, postmodern air, further enhanced by Dave Stewart's keyboards. The jazz-rock turns psychedelic while incorporating a funky groove that keeps things fresh; then Amanda Parsons enters, singing atonally, sounding forever ethereal, like the soundtrack to a gateway into another dimension. Her style differs from how Annette Peacock might sound with Bill Bruford's band, yet she also possesses a quality reminiscent of Sally Oldfield.The music supports her, and subsequently, she supports the music, through both the up-tempo passages and the moments where the action pauses and both the guitar and her voice explore high registers. The composition elevates the piece beyond any single genre. That sense of confusi�n, and the intent of social critique during a turbulent era, also translates into the music and forms an integral part of it.Frank Zappa's One Size Fits All is another essential reference, as are all the bands Stewart was involved with, from Arzachel and Egg, with their classical influences, to the power of Khan alongside Steve Hillage. "Brujo" reveals another facet of the band, featuring Amanda Parsons channeling Annie Haslam; the action is driven simultaneously by her vocals, bass, and keyboards, before shifting into jazz-style improvisation. This album is packed with music, and it shows, as fleeting piano passages give way to keyboards played at breakneck speed that never cease to offer up new melodies, delivering the best of a live concert experience within a studio setting.One could say that the jazz-rock style of "Borogoves" is certainly obscure and intricate, perhaps akin to Brand X, yet Dave Stewart plays the clavinet there, bringing back a funky feel, while Phil Miller's distorted guitar seems to weave through the spaces left open for it. However, its follow-up, "Borogoves, Part One", moves away from those cited references; once again, it is the composition itself that lends the piece its distinctive character and individuality. There is a martial, existentialist quality to the music, heightened, of course, by Amanda Parsons' vocals.Following an initial cacophony of keyboards, "Elephants" serves as a showcase for Phil Miller, before Dave Stewart alternates with his own prowess on acoustic and electric piano, joined by Nick Levitt's synthesizers, delivering fusion riffs that would not only set a precedent but define an era. Jazz-rock had never come so close to being orchestral and symphonic, at least not within the sonic framework established by National Health on their debut, which was rooted in the Canterbury compositional style.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There are many versions of Soft Machine, but only one Allan Holdsworth. There is the Soft Machine of Kevin Ayers, the one with Robert Wyatt, the era featuring Mike Ratledge and Elton Dean, and the later period with Karl Jenkins. Yet Holdsworth brought his signature sound to groups like Tony Williams' Lifetime and Nucleus, as well as later projects such as U.K. and Bill Bruford's solo band. Which brings us to Bundles, where he would also share the bill with bassist Roy Babbington, with whom he had worked on the 1972 Nucleus album Belladonna.While the style of fusion they were developing was already becoming increasingly electrified, Holdsworth's arrival brought powerful riffs that, combined with Mike Ratledge's synthesizers and organ, shaped the main suite, "Hazard Profile." The guitar scales are underpinned by Roy Babbington's tireless bass and Rhodes piano notes that drift like butterflies against the sky of 1975; the truly transcendent moment is the ensuing sequence, aided by the organ, which turns Holdsworth's notes like the pages of a book, gathering layer upon layer of information. One page features virtuosic guitar work that invites us to follow along; another presents piano and acoustic guitar in the suite's second part, capturing the poetic spirit of the era; the fourth section is more intense, almost reminiscent of Cream, save for the syncopated drum rhythm driving the tempo, setting the stage to accelerate into the fifth and final movement, where Karl Jenkins enters on the saxophone.After "Gone Sailing", a track with echoes of Ralph Towner, "Bundles" resumes the initial quest; the guitar navigates curves and corners, venturing into every nook and cranny with clockwork precisi�n, where the drum cymbals act as alarms and the bass serves as the second hand, tirelessly marking the relentless passage of time. The momentum never falters, not even for Holdsworth as "Land of the Bag Snake" begins, since the tracks are seamlessly linked, much like the flowers and privet hedge on the album cover, forming a unified whole where butterflies take flight; "The Man Who Waved at Trains" then continues the journey, albeit at a slower, steady, jazz-infused pace.Karl Jenkins and his oboe provided the missing touch, casting a spell over that timeless afternoon, an afternoon of backyards, plants, and sunshine. Much like on the debut album, the tracks unfold like pages turned by the wind, one after another; amidst this rhythm, Peff enters with keyboards and saxophone, conjuring a dreamlike, otherworldly atmosphere. Where did the violence go? Where did this calm, reminiscent of an endless siesta, come from? It returns through those same instruments, though momentarily clouded by the all-consuming, eternal keyboard. Mike Ratledge and Karl Jenkins vie for the spotlight in the finale, a tour de force where neither truly wins, for the real victor is Soft Machine. "The Floating World" serves as a sort of electronic elegy, a chance to catch one's breath after a relentless journey, an experience that was far from wasted, however, for it undoubtedly leaves the spirit feeling truly fulfilled.

items.body: For Swedish post-punk and goth rock stalwarts Then Comes Silence, songwriting works best when it carries a little danger in its coat pocket, along with a nightclub flyer, a bent cigarette, and perhaps the phone number of somebody your mother warned you about. On Judgement Day, the Stockholm trio take that instinct and feed it through a bright synth opening that sounds almost indecently cheerful before the floor gives way beneath it. The melody initially suggests a lost continental dance hit, polished enough to wander into an airport lounge without being questioned. Then Alex Svenson’s voice enters, carrying the moral weight of a man reading names from a very unpleasant guest list, while Jonas Fransson’s drums and Hugo Zombie’s guitar tighten the track into a stern, muscular march. Clan of Xymox, Killing Joke, and The Chameleons provide useful reference points, though Then Comes Silence retain their own heavy-footed grandeur, where every bass note seems dressed for a funeral, and every hook reads like a majestic elegy for the human race. “This song is about failure, bad decisions and poor behaviour – those who will be the first in line on doomsday,” the band explains. The humor—or perhaps the confession—resides in the arrangement. By featuring an almost alien electronic motif at the outset, the trio playfully embeds their own musical misbehavior, all while enjoying the process. Then Comes Silence greet the end with a crooked smile, loosening goth’s funeral tie and sparing Judgement Day the pallbearer solemnity so often mistaken for depth. Director Damon Zurawski of Future Legends Films places the band among dancers drawn from the gothic scene, creating a performance video that feels communal without sanding down the song’s severity. Svenson commands the center with bass in hand, Fransson drives from behind the kit, and Zombie cuts through the room with economical force. The dancers supply movement, personality, and proof that black clothing contains more shades than most paint stores. Watch the video for Judgement Day below: Judgement Day introduces Requiem Ballroom, due out on November 20th on Metropolis Records. The album follows 2024’s Trickery, a record Classic Rock described as “the post-punk influence of Bauhaus or Joy Division offset by an ’80s windblown, cinematic sense of drama presented with silky production and confidence.” Vive Le Rock concurred, remarking on its “huge, spectral sound that cascades the post-punk genres seamlessly whilst delivering a unique and compelling sound that is as captivatingly gripping as it is intense.” After years of stages shared with Fields of the Nephilim, Clan of Xymox, Chameleons, and A Place to Bury Strangers, Then Comes Silence sound firmly in possession of their machinery. Judgement Day turns failure into propulsion, poor behavior into choreography, and doomsday into a club night worth attending before the lights come up and the bill inevitably comes due at dawn. Then Comes Silence are on tour in mainland Europe in August and September, including an appearance at the M’era Luna Festival in Hildesheim, Germany on 9th August. items.body: I’m taking a ride with my best friend’s girlfriend, and she used to be mine. Love crime. Detroit duo Credit Card make music for the hour when the club floor has acquired the adhesive properties of flypaper, the strobe has erased everyone’s face, and somebody in a leather jacket is conducting a one-sided argument with a subwoofer. Their new single, Love Crime, finds Shaun Hunter handling vocals, synth, and noise while Max Dameron supplies programming, synth, and guitar. Together, they turn romantic misconduct into a hard, queasy sprint through downtown. Love Crime is the second single from Credit Card’s forthcoming debut album, Devil’s Night / Dead Internet, due August 14, 2026. The title suggests either a municipal emergency or the browser history of a recently divorced nightclub promoter, which is more or less the territory the duo occupies. Their synth punk is aggressive, distorted, and built for physical response, though the song’s real pressure comes from the dawning suspicion that desire has selected the worst available route and locked the doors, and nobody involved appears eager to slow down. The sludginess of their sound brings to mind Nine Inch Nails as well as the Soft Moon – it is hypnotic in is raw power. The setup is luridly simple. A man takes a nighttime drive with his best friend’s girlfriend, who also happens to be his former lover. Betrayal, jealousy, and old possession rights crowd into the back seat, where nobody has remembered to fasten a seat belt. The ride carries the thrill of stolen intimacy, yet every beat pushes the characters closer to the embarrassing conclusion that wanting someone can be less a grand passion than a very efficient method of ruining several friendships at once. Hunter delivers the vocal with a cold, accusatory focus, sounding equally implicated and appalled. Dameron’s programming presses forward in blunt mechanical surges, while the synths bend around the rhythm with sinister, sinuous purpose. Guitar and noise roughen the edges without smothering the hook. The result feels immediate and dangerous, like overhearing a confession through the bathroom wall and realizing the names are familiar. On Love Crime, Credit Card makes bad judgment sound fast, stylish, and briefly irresistible. The song understands that romance often provides its own getaway vehicle, though it remains notably unreliable when the police lights appear in the mirror. Listen to Love Crime below and order the single here. Devil’s Night / Dead Internet by CREDIT CARDCredit Card has been building considerable attention in Detroit through shows governed by strobe lights, mosh pits, leather jackets, and beats capable of troubling nearby foundations. Their first seven-inch single, “(CC)” (a Germs reference) sold out at its release show, leaving the group with the enviable problem of having insufficient merchandise and an increasingly attentive audience. Credit Card is readying their debut “mixtape” for a Summer 2026 release, and local crowds in Detroit already sound eager to be flattened by it. Follow Credit Card: Instagram Bandcamp The post “Let’s Go for a Ride” — Detroit Industrial-Punk Duo Credit Card Shares New Single “Love Crime” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: Los Angeles electro-pop duo Tart Vandelay releases its debut album, “Odyssey”, independently on August 7, 2026, on all streaming platforms. The record, made by musical couple Kate Halligan and Marty LoFaso, brings together eleven tracks written and developed over nearly ten years. Halligan stated: “This album is almost like a child to us. It grew up alongside us. Each song captures a different phase of our lives, our relationship, and our evolution as artists and as people. It’s about sharing our art and spreading good vibes to our audience.” LoFaso stated: “Odyssey is proof that it’s worth patiently pursuing a dream. We’re incredibly happy to finally present this first chapter of our story.” ‘Spin,’ ‘Bells’ and ‘Starlight’ lead into ‘Odyssey’ Tart Vandelay built up to “Odyssey” with a run of singles, each presenting a different side of the duo’s sound. “Spin” and “Bells” arrived first, followed by “Starlight,” the final single before the album and, according to the band, the song that ended up setting the creative direction for the whole record. “Starlight” combines synthesizers and pop melodies in an arrangement that balances retro-leaning tones with contemporary production. Across “Odyssey,” the duo mixes synth-pop, electronic indie and contemporary disco into a single identity. “Bells,” the most recent single before “Odyssey,” is available to stream below. About Tart Vandelay Tart Vandelay formed in 2014 when Kate Halligan and Marty LoFaso began writing songs together while studying in Boston; the pair transferred to Berklee College of Music, where Halligan studied songwriting and LoFaso studied music business. The duo later moved to Halligan and LoFaso’s home region in the Northeast before relocating to Phoenix, Arizona, and eventually to Los Angeles, California, where they are now based. Along the way they released the EP “Janus” (2019) and singles including “Luv Who U R” (2021), “DJ Play My Song” (2021), “R U Mine?” (2022) and “I’m Dreaming” (2024), building an independent career around a sound that mixes synth-pop, electronic indie and contemporary disco. In 2026, the singles “Spin” and “Bells” led into “Starlight,” the final single ahead of “Odyssey,” the duo’s debut studio album, released independently on August 7, 2026.

items.body: La Division Technique, the French electronics project of Philippe Saintlos, releases “L’inversion des pôles” with Pascal Comelade as a limited, numbered 7″ vinyl edition of 200 copies through Ubahn. The record is out now. L’inversion des pôles by La Division Technique avec Pascal Comelade La Division Technique and Comelade press two tracks to a numbered 7 inch “L’inversion des pôles” holds two tracks, “Anaphores” on the A side and “Syncopes” on the B side, both composed by Comelade and Saintlos. Comelade plays grand piano, vertical piano, Farfisa organ, an Emenee plastic guitar and a Roland RD 300 SX keyboard, with “Syncopes” adding an EMS-AKS synthesizer and a Koma Elektronik FT201. Saintlos contributes a Korg MS10, an Arturia MiniBrute, a Nord Lead X2, a Yamaha RX11 drum machine, an ARP Odyssey and a Poly D clone Minimoog. The two recorded the pair of tracks with Raph Dumas between November 2024 and April 2026; Dumas also mastered the release, and Saintlos produced it and designed the sleeve. Each of the 200 copies is individually numbered. About La Division Technique La Division Technique is an electronics project from France, founded and directed by Philippe Saintlos, built around old-school electronics, dark soundscapes, minimal synths and industrial-ambient textures played on analog synthesizers, filters, guitars, voices and spatial sound recordings. A 2017 meeting with the label Rotorelief led to the release of the album “Unexpected Works, Random Systems,” drawn from tape recordings dating to the 1980s. A second album, “Nebula,” followed in 2019 on Rotorelief and Ubahn. The project returned in 2023 with “Traversant les cités liquides,” and issued “Tristes Machines,” its fourth album, on Ubahn in 2025, alongside the 2024 single “A Beginners Guide to Brian Eno…Baby’s On Fire.” Saintlos has also co-founded the labels Ditec, Semantic and Odessa. Pascal Comelade, born in Montpellier in 1955, is a self-taught French Catalan musician who debuted with the electronic-leaning album “Fluences,” influenced by Heldon, before building a body of work centered on toy instruments played through his Bel Canto Orquestra; he has recorded with Robert Wyatt, Faust, Christophe Miossec and P.J. Harvey among others. His work with La Division Technique on “L’inversion des pôles” pairs his toy-instrument and acoustic keyboard playing with Saintlos’s analog synthesizer sound.

items.body: The Copenhagen-based Institute for the Criminally Insane (ICI) and Danish dark synth act ee:man release the EBM/electro-industrial single “Born to Ride..” on August 14, 2026 through Tinnitorturous. The digital single arrives on major streaming and download services, with a lossless version on both acts’ Bandcamp pages. It is the second collaboration single by Institute for the Criminally Insane and ee:man, following “The Fabric of You..”. “Born to Ride..” addresses taking a fall, making a turn and getting back on your feet, set to music that is slower and darker than its predecessor. The cover was designed by Bo Heidelberg. ‘Born to Ride..’ follows ICI and ee:man’s ‘The Fabric of You..’ Institute for the Criminally Insane and ee:man first paired up on “The Fabric of You..”, released on Tinnitorturous. “Born to Ride..” carries the collaboration forward with a heavier, more subdued arrangement than the earlier single. Both acts’ back catalogues, including ICI’s “Gekippt” and ee:man’s “Bite the Hand,” remain available on their respective Bandcamp pages. About Institute for the Criminally Insane Institute for the Criminally Insane formed in Copenhagen in 1988. The project released its first compilation of demos, “Demo,” in 1990, followed by the EP “Audiotherapy” in 1993 and the album “Gekippt” in 1994, both through the now-defunct Danish label Decay Records. “Gekippt” became a cult album internationally, and its track “Slasher” was used in the video game “Hitman: Blood Money.” Institute for the Criminally Insane originally consisted of Bo Heidelberg and Kim G. Hansen. Bo Heidelberg reignited the project in 2020 and was briefly joined by Simon Holm before continuing as a one-man project. Institute for the Criminally Insane is currently working on material for release on Tinnitorturous and the Australian label Lightarmour Editions. ee:man is the Danish dark synth act of a producer who debuted in 2021 with the album “Echoes of Life,” built on melancholy synth chords and industrial undertones, and has been compared to Recoil, the solo project of Depeche Mode’s Alan Wilder. In recent years ee:man has moved toward EBM and industrial territory through collaborations with acts including In Absentia and Negant, and previously released the single “Bite the Hand” in January 2026. His darker material appears on Tinnitorturous, a Danish label run by Jens B. Petersen (ManMindMachine, Negant) and Tommy B-Kuhlmann (In Absentia, Negant, Body-Banden), while his lighter synth pop work is released through Town & Towers Records. “Born to Ride..” marks the second collaboration single between Institute for the Criminally Insane and ee:man.

items.body: Finnish Electronic Punk duo I Think I Broke Something releases the single “Illegal” on August 6. The track is the first single from the duo’s upcoming EP “Another Escape,” due November 5 on the same day as a release show at Semifinal in Helsinki. Illegal by I Think I Broke Something “Illegal” continues the sound the duo has built its catalog on, pairing electronic production with heavier, metal-weighted instrumentation. “Illegal continues ITIBS’s signature blend of explosive electronics and metal-heavy weight. Someone once described our sound as The Prodigy on steroids. And this track probably sounds exactly like that,” the band states. ‘Illegal’ leads into ‘Another Escape’ and a Helsinki release show “Illegal” is the first taste of “Another Escape,” the duo’s next EP, out November 5. The band will mark the EP’s release the same day with a show at Semifinal in Helsinki. Sonically, “Illegal” sits alongside prior ITIBS singles such as “Raw” and “Corpse”, continuing a distorted electronic hybrid the band places somewhere between The Prodigy, 3TEETH and Nine Inch Nails. About I Think I Broke Something I Think I Broke Something, also known as ITIBS, is a Helsinki-based duo made up of Jouni and Miika, active since 2014. The project debuted with the EP “Superman Sabotage Clan” and has since released three full-length albums, including “Still Not Going To” on October 26, 2022, alongside numerous singles and remixes through various labels. Prior singles from that album cycle included “Astral” and “All Is Not,” the latter remixed by drum’n’bass and metal producer Zardonic. The duo has also worked with The Prodigy’s Maxim and DJ Hyper. ITIBS describes its sound as a distorted electronic hybrid drawing on The Prodigy, Skinny Puppy and 3TEETH, mixing explosive electronics with metal-heavy weight. “Illegal,” released August 6, extends that catalog and leads into the EP “Another Escape,” due November 5 alongside the band’s release show at Semifinal in Helsinki.

items.body: Eye New Dark, the synthpop and darkwave solo project of Null Device vocalist and keyboardist Jill Sheridan, released the five-track EP “Adore” digitally on 4 August 2026 via Bandcamp. The EP follows Sheridan’s description of the project as built on “dark melodies, synthy beats.” Adore by Eye New Dark ‘Adore’ tracklist and prior single “Adore” contains five tracks: “More than Perfect,” “Real Life,” “Backwards Through That Door,” “A-D-O-R-E” and “Eyes in the Dark.” The third track previously appeared as a standalone single, “Backwards Through That Door,” released 30 June 2026 with two remixes: one by Klack and one by Null Device. Those remixes are not included on “Adore,” which presents the original version of the song alongside four new tracks. “Adore” is Eye New Dark’s second release. Sheridan introduced the project in May 2024 with the four-track “Tell Me / Smile My Dear,” which also carried remixes from Klack and Null Device. About Eye New Dark Eye New Dark is the solo project of Jill Sheridan, who has served as keyboardist, vocalist, songwriter and producer in Null Device since the Madison, Wisconsin band’s founding in 1995 by University of Wisconsin students Eric Oehler, Eric Goedken and Sheridan herself. Null Device moved from instrumental electronic music toward the romantic, New Order-referencing synthpop that has defined the band since, signing to Nilaihah Records in 2002 and releasing a run of albums that incorporated Arabic and Indian instrumentation before the label’s dissolution. The band went on to self-release two further records and later signed to Distortion Productions, issuing “While You Were Otherwise Engaged” in December 2016 and the eighth album, “The Emerald Age”, in November 2022. Sheridan launched Eye New Dark alongside her continuing role in Null Device, debuting the project in May 2024 with “Tell Me / Smile My Dear.” “Adore,” released in August 2026, is the project’s first five-track EP and its second overall release. No Wikipedia entry or Discogs profile exists yet specifically for Eye New Dark.

items.body: “Incarnate” marks the third album from the American band False Figure, with the trio delivering eleven tracks on this release. The band’s influences clearly hark back to the golden era of the 80s, spanning various—although closely related—genres. Dark-Wave elements are immediately recognizable, primarily brought to life through the guitar work, alongside subtle traces of Shoegaze. At times, the sound leans more towards Rock, while there are even passages reminiscent of Jangle-Pop—think Aztec Camera. It feels like an imaginary meeting point between The Cure, Joy Division, The Smiths, The Jesus & Mary Chain, and Aztec Camera. “Incarnate” is a diverse record, featuring several standout tracks. This variety makes for an accessible listening experience, ensuring that there is something to appeal to a wide range of listeners. Despite its stylistic diversity, the album never feels disjointed; rather, it comes across as a tight and cohesive production. False Figure was not a band I was particularly familiar with, but this release has certainly won me over. (Rating:7½). Side-Line reported on the False Figure release “Incarnate” on Cruel Subordination Records in March 2026, detailing the tracklist and the limited vinyl pressing. Watch the clip “Say Nothing”: About False Figure False Figure started as a Bay Area three-piece built around Andrés Ruiz (guitar, vocals), with Ian on drums and Alex on bass. In 2017, the band self-released the 7″ single “Cardinal Cross b/w Exhale”. A self-titled album followed on May 25, 2018, released by Near Dark Records and Last Hour Records. On June 11, 2019, the band released the EP “A Promised End.” Later cassette pressings followed via Reclusion Records and Transylvanian Recordings. On November 1, 2022, the band released “Castigations.” Three years later, in late 2025 and early 2026, the band issued advance tracks for “Incarnate,” including “Flowers in Bloom,” released on January 29, 2026. For “Incarnate” the line-up consisted of Kevin Defranco (guitars), Kienan Hamilton (bass guitar), and Andrés Ruiz (vocals, guitars, drum programming, keys). The album, released via Cruel Subordination Records on digital, vinyl, and cassette formats, is the band’s third full-length.

items.body: August has landed, and Dutch summer firmly has me in it’s clammy paws. As I sit here, sweating out an unseasonable bout of some mysterious illness, a chilling, forest-dwelling revenant beckons. Seeking solace in the shade of mist-shrouded pines, I accept her invitation and am transported from the muggy heat of these low lands to the forests of the Pacific Northwest. Folk and death metal infused black metal project Hulder is her name, and her frontwoman Marliese Beeuwsaert has taken this journey physically. Since starting the project in 2018, she has moved across the Atlantic— leaving Belgium for the PNW—and added bassist/shared vocalist Necreon to the bands official line-up.Hulder’s previous record Verses in Oath (2024) briefly drew me into its orbit based on some favourable coverage in my regular haunts, and then quite quickly disappeared back behind the treeline, leaving impressions of some inspired riffs and passages and an unusually meaty, Swedeath-leaning guitar tone. It lacked a certain melodic memorability and iconic key moments to latch onto, and while at first I suspected these might shimmer into perspective out of the gloam on repeat listens, such revelation never descended from the canopy. It was with intrigue but tempered expectations that I embarked upon the dark and crooked woodland paths of Verbolgen (which according to sources translates to "Incensed", although that lacks a certain simmering resentfulness; I’d go for something in between that, like resentful, and spiteful).After a neither offensive nor particularly memorable intro, Hulder come out of the gate quite strong, with opening one-two punch “The Crowning” and “Thy Binding Oath” showing the band's fresh shoots of folk instrumentation, still supported by dark, rhythmic undergrowth and thick, gnarled trunks of riffs, vocals howling through the branches like a biting north wind. To my mild disappointment, however, the album’s promising start loses its footing and stumbles over hidden roots and in musty burrows. As soon as the tracks revert to shorter, faster and more blackened fare, they land unfortunately between melodic and biting, offering neither grandiose mysticism nor blistering assault. Around the album’s halfway point, the moonlit clearing that opens “In Blood and in Earth” and leads toward a more deliberate, slower movement shows significant promise, although the track and Verbolgen as a whole remain rooted in a similar issue as Verses in Oath was. These albums are certainly very well performed and produced, and clearly feature a personal touch being themed around Belgian folklore and adorned with multilingual lyrics.The album's second half features some glimmers of tantalizing starlight, most notably on the vicious riffs and melodic developments of “Den Nacht Zijn Lied” ("Night’s Song") which may hold up as the strongest track. “View From Nemeton” has some strong moments, and “A Beacon From Darkened Skies” comes perhaps closest to the kind of grand and layered melodic payoff that I expect from an album in this style. The interesting closing bonus track “Zonnesteen” ("Sunstone") leans hard into acoustic folk sensibilities, but unfortunately fails to weave their strands into a satisfying wreath with which to adorn the finished product. Whatever lingers in between the tracks I’ve mentioned unfortunately fails to become more than tantalizing silhouettes in the mist. Having traversed its sylvan bounds, Verbolgen was a bit of a frustrating album to review. Stylistically it ticks all my boxes, the production is excellent, and musicians both new and old, guest and permanent show they have what it takes. Hulder have clearly been hard at work further carving out their sound without endangering its promising heartwood. Yet, capitalizing on that promise with an album full of songs whose resin sticks to the soul as much as it smells inviting remains tantalisingly out of reach on Verbolgen, just as it did on Verses in Oath. I fear this album will also slip out of rotation soon, although I intend to give it some more time to gestate. Perhaps when the seasons change, it will appear favorable in dwindling light.  Verbolgen by Hulder

items.body: Within progressive music, and especially within its odd sister-genre zeuhl, there are many competing forces. This makes sense, of course: a genre known for musical experimentation must, by force, include contradiction because that's how our brains often perceive complexity. Especially in music, where the competing forces of harmony and dissonance make up so much of our perception. Specifically in progressive rock, we can identify a few central tensions: melody, dissonance, tightness, expansiveness, and more. Papangu first burst into our perception with Holoceno, an album that was a sort of conflagration created from all of these tensions being driven to their brink. They followed that up with Lampião Rei, which was journey down one path, namely one of "open", "thin", and expansiveness sounds. Now, the Brazilian ensemble returns with another version, this time reaching deep into the core of progressive rock and bringing back one of its most defining attributes: brightness.Where Holoceno was tight like a ball of magma and Lampião Rei was rarified like a cloud, Celestial takes after its namesake and shines like the sun or the stars. First and foremost in creating this brightness are the synths. Instead of the all encompassing and redolent sound of Holoceno, Celestial is characterized with a sweet, warm, and fantastical synth sound which immediately sets the stage for exploration. Fans of progressive rock will immediately reach for the Yes comparison but there is more here than simple homage; Papangu are proving themselves masters of this sound as well, creating truly engrossing and captivating passages with the synths. My favorites are on "Colosso", the second track, an agile, light-hearted, and transportive affair that works wonders on the heart.It also has great usage of my second favorite on this album: bass. Papangu have chosen a "natural" and rich tone to couple with the synths here and "Colosso" has some of the best "conversations" between synth and bass that I've heard. Of course the guitars and the drums play a major role in these discussions; the drums are especially important for this track, and for the album. But there is something so joyous in how the bass and synths work here, something in their agility and subtilty that communicates the main accent or theme of the album. "Celeste", further down the album, is another magnificent example of this collaboration and probably my favorite track on the album in its whirling, jittery pace.In a way, this lighter tone serves to make Celestial feel more approachable and less intricate but this, of course, is a mistake. With a ten-part concept at its core, and multiple genres swimming within its embrace, Celestial has a lot of intricacy to it. In a way, it is less accessible because it is also less upfront with its ambition. It requires that the listener commit fully to its journey, a staple of the sort of progressive rock being referenced here. Luckily, this is quite easy to do as the album reveals more and more of its beauty on repeated listens. We haven't covered even a fragment of what's waiting for you on Celestial, from mysterious vocals, through breakneck grooves and folks sensibilities, and all the way to fusion rock and psychedelic crescendos. If you clicked on this review, you probably already knew I was only going to be able to capture a slight part of one of progressive rock's most intricate bands and you were right. Papangu have once more released a work of music on their own terms, completely dedicated to their craft and its execution. Its a different path up the mountain but oh boy, is the view just as gorgeous, awash in the rays of a bright, warm sun promising many valleys and peaks before the journey is done. Step forwards, won't you? Celestial by Papangu Celestial will be released on August 7th. You can, and should, click through to the Bandcamp link above to pre-order it.
